title: Near-optimal quantum simulation of lattice Lindbladian dynamics
authors: Rahul Trivedi, Xiehang Yu, Daniel Malz
abstract: We consider the problem of simulating dynamics under geometrically local Lindbladians acting on a lattice of qudits. We present an algorithm to approximate the time evolution under these Lindbladians for evolution time $t$ and on $N$ qudits to diamond norm error $\varepsilon$ using geometrically local circuits of depth $O(t \ \polylog(Nt/\varepsilon))$. Our results thus achieve a performance comparable to that of the Haah-Hastings-Kothari-Low (HHKL) algorithm for lattice Hamiltonian simulation.
summary: This paper presents a near-optimal quantum algorithm to simulate dynamics governed by Lindbladian master equations on a lattice. By utilizing the exact dilation into a system-environment unitary evolution, the authors adapt techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to handle the irreversible nature of open quantum systems. This achieves scaling comparable to state-of-the-art methods, making it highly relevant for quantum simulation of dissipative processes.
main_problem: Developing quantum algorithms to simulate time evolution under geometrically local Lindbladians efficiently.
main_result: The authors present a near-optimal algorithm achieving gate depth $O(t 	ext{ polylog}(Nt/\epsilon))$, matching the performance of HHKL for Hamiltonian simulation.
method: The approach involves using an exact dilation of the Lindblad master equation via Quantum Stochastic Calculus and then applying techniques analogous to those used for Hamiltonian simulation.
model_or_system: The system is a lattice of qudits whose dynamics are governed by a Lindbladian master equation $\mathcal{L} = \sum_e L_e$. The simulation is performed by mapping the Lindbladian evolution to a unitary evolution of an extended system-environment state.
key_observables: Approximation error in the diamond norm ($\lVert E - \exp(Lt) Vert_\diamond \le \epsilon$), and the required gate complexity.
important_parameters: Evolution time ($t$), system size ($N$), and approximation error ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The analysis requires bounding the environment state to a low-excitation subspace and relies on constructing efficient block-encodings for the system-environment dynamics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dilation of the Lindblad evolution, showing how jump operators couple the system to independent bosonic fields, and how the system-environment interaction is modeled.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem using the Lindbladian and its dilation. It then develops techniques to bound the system-environment interaction within a low-excitation space, culminating in the construction of unitaries using block-encoding and polar factor approximations to achieve the final complexity bounds.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses simulating open quantum systems (Lindbladians) on quantum hardware, which is a major challenge in quantum computation, by adapting successful techniques from Hamiltonian simulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Dilation of the Lindblad evolution. Each jump operator Lα couples the system S to an independent bosonic field through a† α(t)Lα + h.c.. With all fields initially in the vacuum, tracing out the environment recovers the system’s Lindblad dynamics.

Figure 2: Dilation of nearest-neighbour Lindblad dynamics on a chain. Each edge term Le is represented by a system–environment interaction He(t) involving the two adjacent sites (blue disks) and ancillary bosonic fields (pink rectangles). The fields start in the vacuum and are traced out after the joint unitary evolution U(t,s), with t ≥s.

Figure 3: Local splitting of the system–environment evolution. (a) Regions A, B, and C, with boundary interactions H(∂) A,B and H(∂) B,C. (b) The full evolution is approximated by evolution on B ∪C, backward evolution on B, and evolution on A ∪B. The environment is retained throughout all three operations and traced out only at the end.
Figure 4: Three-layer decomposition of the dilated evolution. Each layer comprises unitaries that factorize over blocks of width at most 2l. In the final algorithm, l = O(log(Nt/ε)).

Figure 5: Collision-model approximation (right) of a sequence of forward and backward system– environment evolutions (left). The bosonic fields are replaced by ancillary qubits associated with time bins of width δ. Each ancillary qubit is used three times: first during forward evolution, again during the corresponding backward time step and a third time in the final forward time step. In the end, the ancillary qubits are traced out.
